ICYMI - Thursday Finance with David Chau
Yesterday, a rebound in gold and copper prices drove ASX-listed mining stocks sharply higher, and Wall Street experienced another volatile session after huge swings for tech companies.
David Chau has Thursday's recap:
Domestic gas reservation scheme is law, with hope of a turn-around in manufacturing
We're going to keep more gas here.

A domestic gas reservation scheme means exporters will have to set aside up to 20% of their exports (from 2028) for domestic use. That will reduce energy prices and aims to stop what's been a shuttering of manufacturing, as local makers have seen prices become uneconomic.

It ends a pretty wild situation, where we've been one of the world's largest exporters of liquified natural gas (LNG) at the same time as watching manufacturing plants close because they can't get access to enough of the fuel.
This is an east coast problem.
WA has had its own gas reservation policy for two decades, which has helped to insulate its economy from the price shocks experienced on the east coast.
One of the loudest and longest proponents of this shift has been the Australian Workers' Union (AWU).
A media release says the AWU has "campaigned relentlessly for a gas reservation scheme for 14 years".
But it must be longer.

I remember sitting in the AWU's Melbourne office as the concept was explained to me, with the union's then-boss Bill Shorten across the floor in another room. He entered parliament in 2007 (and went on to become leader of the ALP) so if my memory is correct it must have been before that!
AWU National Secretary Paul Farrow said the impact of today’s vote in the Senate would be felt for generations.
"We have known for a long time that a gas reservation scheme was necessary, but successive Australian governments were bullied and manipulated by multinational gas exporters.
"This government is the first in a generation to stand up to the gas lobby and tell them that the national interest must come first.
"Certainly the best time to introduce an Australian gas reservation scheme was over a decade ago. But the next best time is now.

"Today marks a long-overdue turning point for Australian industry. Australia's natural gas wealth should be a tailwind for our manufacturing sector. Today we finally give our domestic manufacturers the advantage they should have had from the beginning.
"Australian industry has been battered for over a decade by high gas costs. Thousands of blue-collar jobs have been lost unnecessarily. Today there is hope of a turnaround.

"My members know they work in a country that produces more gas than just about anywhere else. And yet they've watched factory after factory shut because they couldn’t access affordable gas. It's been a national disgrace.

"On behalf of every AWU member I congratulate the government and parliament for passing this legislation. You have paved the way for Australia to reclaim its place as a global force in manufacturing."
We've been covering the rise in gas costs — and the impact — for a long time. It will be fascinating to see if things change from 2028.
Key Event
Changing of the guard at Macquarie Bank
A changing of the guard at Macquarie, with two of its most senior executives announcing their retirement this morning.
Macquarie Bank chief executive Stuart Green and Macquarie Group chief operating officer Nicole Sorbara will step down from the executive committee at the end of March next year.
Amy Mahony, currently chief risk officer at Macquarie Asset Management, will take over as the bank's CEO, while Tony Graham will assume Ms Sorbara's technology responsibilities and become CIO.
Macquarie Group chief executive Greg Ward said this about the outgoing executives:

"Over 25 years, Stuart has had meaningful impact through several key periods of growth and industry challenge as Head of Investor Relations, Group Treasurer and over the last six years as MBL Managing Director and CEO, and as a member of the MBL Board.

"Meanwhile, Nicole's 30-year career across finance, Macquarie Capital, as Global Head of Human Resources and for the last 14 years as COO, saw a meaningful uplift in our technology and operations, supporting the global growth and diversification of our business and making a major contribution to Macquarie's culture, not least through the landmark workplaces she developed around the world, including our Metro Martin Place global headquarters in Sydney."
The competition watchdog's tips for using AI tools to shop
Before relying on AI-powered tools to compare, choose, buy or get advice, consumers should remember:

• Check important answers with a reliable source. AI tools can sound confident and still be wrong. Check information beyond AI before acting on it. This is particularly important when making choices about your health, legal rights, significant purchases and financial commitments, or safety.
• Check what information is missing. If AI recommends the "best" product, service or price, independently verify this through an online search.
• Protect personal information. Think carefully before putting financial, medical, identity or other personal or sensitive information into an AI tool, and understand how it can use your information.

• Think before letting AI act on your behalf. Before allowing an AI agent to take action on your behalf, think carefully about the permissions and instructions you give the tool. Always verify financial transactions and other important actions before an AI agent takes these on your behalf.
• You can still ask for human help. If an AI chatbot can't resolve a complaint, or understand your circumstances, escalate the issue. Keep screenshots or a record of important interactions.
Key Event
Are you using AI to help you shop for deals during the Black Friday sales? The ACCC is warning to think & check
The ACCC has issued a fresh warning about the use of AI, including AI assistants to shop for deals during Black Friday sales.

There are many 'personal assistant' AI agents already available on the Australian market, such as Meta's Muse, OpenAI's ChatGPT dots and Google Tasks. These products can integrate with services such as consumers' email, cloud storage and banking and they can act for a consumer.
"Many consumers value the ability of AI to quickly compare different options and make recommendations, and newer AI products are able to make purchases," ACCC Chair Gina Cass-Gottlieb said.
"But while using AI can make life easier, AI results can be wrong. Consumers need to take care when using AI for research and when asking AI agents to act on their behalf.

"Before allowing an AI agent to buy products, consumers should check what personal information it can access, and think carefully about the permissions and instructions they give it so they can control how much it can spend. Consumers should check and set the points at which they want the agent to get their approval.

"Consumers using AI tools to research products should remember an AI tool can sound confident and certain despite being wrong. An AI tools' answer to questions can be different at different times, and it can also be open to manipulation or reflect biases in its training data," Ms Cass-Gottlieb said.
"So, we are advising consumers to also check information directly — such as on a sellers' website — especially if they are considering a significant purchase."
Consumers should also watch for AI-cloned storefronts and deepfake brand or celebrity advertisements and exercise caution before completing purchases.
The ACCC says product images and descriptions created using generative AI can make products appear of a higher quality than they are and may also not accurately identify something is a scam.
Gold is at a 14-month low, what is the outlook?
A little over a year ago, FOMO had people lining up for hours to get their hands on the precious metal.
At one stage, the price was more than $US5,400 an ounce.
The frenzy saw the traditional relationship between gold and US interest rates break down as fear of missing out took over.
But in the last year or so, gold has lost more than a third of its value.
Take a watch of this excellent interview between The Business's Alicia Barry and ABC Bullion general manager Jordan Eliseo.
Investors return to tech stocks, but will the recovery last?
Some calm has returned to global markets after a volatile week, with European shares rallying overnight while Wall Street took a break for Thanksgiving.
Investors have been snapping up technology and chip stocks again, while miners, banks and automakers also enjoyed a solid session in Europe.
But NAB’s economists are cautious about whether the improvement in investor confidence will last.

"The dip buying in the US equity market into Wednesday's close has been enough to calm investor sentiment, resulting in a risk positive trading session overnight," NAB said in its morning markets note."In the absence of any new information the backdrop does remain fragile but for now investors have returned to equities with technology shares leading – European semiconductor sector surging."

"In the absence of any new information the backdrop does remain fragile but for now investors have returned to equities with technology shares leading – European semiconductor sector surging."
The next big test will come when Wall Street reopens, futures for both the S&P 500 and Nasdaq 100 are pointing higher.
Key Event
Spain’s Pablo Hernández de Cos nominated as next ECB president
Eurozone countries have selected former Spanish central bank governor Pablo Hernández de Cos to succeed Christine Lagarde as president of the European Central Bank.
The 55-year-old economist currently heads the Bank for International Settlements and is regarded as a pragmatic and moderate policymaker.
Analysts say his appointment is unlikely to signal a major shift in monetary policy, as the ECB grapples with a resurgence in inflation and concerns about political instability in France.
Subject to formal confirmation, Hernández de Cos will take over when Lagarde steps down on February 7, chairing his first interest rate meeting on March 18.
EU leaders are expected to give the appointment their final approval at a summit in December.
ASX set to open higher
On the home run for the work week, happy Friday all.
Lin Lin from the ABC business team here to take you through the morning's events.
Wall Street was closed for Thanksgiving holiday, but shares in Europe rebounded (STOXX rising by nearly 2%) after solid gains across Asia.
ASX futures are pointing to a rise of 0.1% as at 7am AEDT.
Millions of Australians will be hunting for a bargain in the coming days as the Black Friday and Cyber Monday sales period reaches fever pitch.
But the ACCC has been out and about in recent weeks cautioning consumers about sneaky marketing tactics that could lead shoppers to think they are getting bigger savings than they are.
